verification_vocabulary: Same as GRAPH-FORMAT.md: bibliographic_metadata_checked = identity/edition checked against the record named; supporting_page_checked = an abstract, publisher summary, contents page, review text or opening text was read for the specific point in the note; unverified = could not be confirmed, kept out of proposed sources. No book was read in full. Subtitles follow Crossref, Open Library or the citation graph's bibliographic strings; places of publication follow publisher convention and were not separately checked.

records.citation: Carl Berger, The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867–1914 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1970; 2nd ed. 2013).

verification.checked_against: Open Library work OL2446797W (UTP; earliest edition record dated 1971); Crossref record of a review, International Journal 26:1 (1970–71), doi:10.2307/40201036; Crossref DOI and chapter DOIs of the 2013 second edition (contents); for the thesis: 49th Shelf UTP publisher copy (https://49thshelf.com/content/view/full/5186340), Ramsay Cook, Literary Review of Canada, April 2013 (https://reviewcanada.ca/magazine/2013/04/beverley-baxter-in-empireland/), Robert M. Stamp, Project MUSE article 675533 (search snippet only)
verification.note: Contents read (2nd ed.): "Men", "Canada First", "The Loyalist Tradition", "Progress and Liberty", "The Canadian Character", "Critique of the Republic", "Social Criticism and Reform", "Mission", "Militarism". The book's thesis is not read; the first-edition year (1970 vs 1971) should be confirmed. Thesis (added 2026-10-12, partly verified): Berger's formulation that Canadian imperialism was one variety (Stamp) or version (Cook) of Canadian nationalism is known from two later scholars' quotations and the UTP publisher copy ('significantly influenced by its leading advocates' belief in nationalism'); the exact word and page in the 1970 introduction are unchecked, so the draft paraphrases and does not quote.

records.citation: Susan Mann Trofimenkoff, “Nationalism, Feminism & Canadian Intellectual History,” Canadian Literature 83 (Winter 1979): 7–20.

verification.checked_against: Canadian Literature article page and issue record (https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/canlit/article/view/194603; https://ojs.library.ubc.ca/index.php/canlit/issue/view/182629)
verification.note: Full text read (answers/research/q11-intellectual-history-critique.json). Argues Canadian intellectual history, anchored to nationalism and present-minded interest in national unity, implied 'that women are virtually non-existent'; notes most intellectual historians were men and that women's history grew from social history in isolation from it; urges attention to feminist ideas and women's part in forming ideology. Examples mostly French-Canadian; critique covers Cook, Berger and Shortt. Special issue on intellectual history. Karr (1989, n. 6) cites it with the issue misgiven as 93.

records.reading: Feminist critique: a field anchored to nationalism left women nearly invisible.

records.citation: Clarence Karr, “What Happened to Canadian Intellectual History?” Acadiensis 18, no. 2 (Spring 1989): 158–74 (review essay).

verification.checked_against: Acadiensis article page and full text (https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/Acadiensis/article/view/12284; https://journals.lib.unb.ca/index.php/Acadiensis/article/download/12284/13128); Érudit record (https://www.erudit.org/en/journals/acadiensis/1989-v18-n2-acadiensis_18_2/acad18_2re04/)
verification.note: Full text read (answers/research/q11-intellectual-history-critique.json). Analyses the field's 'preoccupation with delineating the national mind', its 'propensity to place everything in an atmosphere of crisis' and 'its narrow, elitist, biographical methodology' (p. 160); group biography after Berger's Sense of Power focuses on 'an elite group composed primarily of academics, journalists and clergymen' (p. 169), leaving little known of what the population thought. Names Berger, McKillop, Cook, Shortt, Levitt, Allen and Francis; calls the books 'excellent studies within their self-imposed context'.

records.reading: Critique: national mind, crisis framing, and an elitist group-biography method.
